---
title: "R12. Algorithmic transparency and AI"
description: "The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard, meaningful human oversight, and using AI tools to do the analysis."
---

Where an algorithmic or AI tool is part of the analysis, three things follow: publishing what
the tool does, keeping a human genuinely in a position to change the outcome, and being clear
about AI used to produce the work.

## Algorithmic transparency

The **Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard** is how a public body publishes what an
algorithmic tool does, what it is for, what data it was built on, how it affects decisions, who is
accountable for it and what oversight it has. It exists because a decision a person cannot
interrogate is a decision they cannot challenge.

**It is mandatory in two steps, and both have to be met.**

**Step 1, the organisation.** The standard is mandatory for all government departments, and for arm's
length bodies which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact with the general
public.[^src-atrs-section-2] NHSBSA does both, so the organisation is in scope. It is recommended
across the rest of the public sector, which is not in mandatory scope.[^src-atrs-section-2]

**Step 2, the tool.** Within an organisation in scope, the standard is mandatory for algorithmic
tools which have **a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect**, or
which **directly interact with the general public**.[^src-atrs-section-2]

::: {.callout-important title="Most of the analysis this playbook covers is outside the mandatory scope" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
The standard says the scope is designed to emphasise context, "focusing on situations where a tool
is influencing specific operational decisions about individuals, organisations or groups, not where
a tool is an analytical model supporting broad government policymaking".[^src-atrs-section-2]

An eligibility rule, a risk score or a triage tool applied to individual cases is the first thing. A
model that informs a policy, a funding settlement or a published statistic is the second. **The test
is what the tool decides, and about whom.** It is not how visible the analysis is, and it is not the
assurance level it scored.

Being outside the mandatory scope is not a reason to publish nothing. The Data and AI Ethics
Framework recommends publishing a record "even where a tool does not strictly fall within scope of
the ATRS".[^src-data-and-ai-ethics-framework-atrs] Read the mandatory scope as the floor rather than
the ceiling.
:::

**Make the check at scoping.** Ask whether the tool is in scope when you agree the work, in the same
conversation that sets the assurance level, and record the answer either way. A record takes
drafting and internal clearance before it can be published, so there needs to be time for that. The two decisions are separate. An analysis can be Level 4 BCA and out of ATRS scope, and it can be
Level 2 Enhanced and in it.

::: {.callout-important title="If you cannot explain it, say so" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
Explainability is an assurance requirement, not a nice-to-have.

Where a method cannot be explained, for example a vendor-supplied scoring tool whose weighting is not
disclosed, **that limitation must be stated in the output**, and where the tool is in scope it
belongs in the record as well.

"We can describe what goes in and what comes out but not how it works" is a finding about the
analysis, and the reader needs it.
:::

The same structured approach to business risk applies to black-box models as to any other. The
difficulty is in transparency, in having the right mix of experts available, and in understanding
what mitigations are possible. It is not a reason to assure them less.

**Who does what.** The standard names two roles. An organisation in mandatory scope has a **single
point of contact**, whose job is to coordinate with the standard's own team. They identify the tools in scope, and they
draft and publish the records. If you do not know who yours is, the guidance gives
[algorithmic-transparency@dsit.gov.uk](mailto:algorithmic-transparency@dsit.gov.uk) as the
address to ask.[^src-atrs-section-2] Each record names a **senior responsible
owner**, given as a role title rather than a person, which is the role ultimately accountable for the
tool in an operational context.[^src-atrs-section-6]

Who holds each of those at NHSBSA is a governance decision rather than something the standard
settles. This playbook proposes that the analyst drafts the record as part of delivery, and that the Head of
Profession for Statistics clears it before publication. A record is a public statement about a tool,
and it needs the same sign-off as a published statistic. That is a proposal, not
a requirement of the standard, and it is on the list at
[who to ask](r3-who-to-ask.qmd).

## Meaningful human oversight

"A human is involved" is not oversight. It is a sentence that can be true while nobody is actually in
a position to change anything.

**The legal floor comes first.** UK GDPR article 22 prohibits decisions based **solely** on automated
processing that have legal or similarly significant consequences for an individual. A service using
an algorithmic tool that affects a person's legal status or rights may only use it to **support** a
decision that a human decision-maker makes.[^src-ai-playbook-human-oversight]

Above that floor, how much human involvement is enough depends on three things: the complexity
of the output, its potential impact, and how much specialist knowledge reading it
requires.[^src-ai-playbook-human-oversight] Design, document and assess the stages where human
review happens, and what further information the reviewer takes into
account.[^src-ai-playbook-human-oversight]

**Five questions make oversight real rather than nominal.**

| Question | Why it is the one that bites |
|---|---|
| **Who reviews the output?** | A named role, not "the team". Oversight nobody owns is oversight nobody does |
| **What authority do they have?** | Can they change the answer, or only note a concern about it |
| **When can they challenge or override?** | Before the decision is acted on, or only after somebody complains |
| **What gets recorded?** | That a review happened, what it considered, and what it changed |
| **Can the decision be reviewed or appealed?** | By the person it was about, and through what route |

If the honest answer to the second question is "none", the first question has not been answered
either, whatever the process document says.

## Using AI tools to do the analysis

This is different from analysis **of** an algorithmic tool. It is the everyday case: an analyst using
an AI assistant to write code, summarise a document, draft a passage or explain an error.

The playbook's position is that **this changes nothing about who is accountable**, and that saying so
plainly is better than leaving it to be worked out one analyst at a time.

- **Use the tools your organisation has approved**, through the route it has approved them. Which
  tools those are is an NHSBSA decision, not one this playbook can make.
- **Do not put data into a tool that is not cleared to hold it.** Patient data, personal data and
  anything under a data sharing agreement are the obvious cases, and the default answer is no unless
  someone with the authority has said yes in writing.
- **Verify what comes back.** An AI output is a statistically informed guess rather than a
  fact.[^src-ai-playbook-accuracy] Code gets tested, a summary gets checked against the source, a
  figure gets recalculated. The verification is the work; the draft was the shortcut.
- **Accountability does not transfer.** The analyst who signs the output owns everything in it. "The
  tool produced it" is not a finding, a caveat or a defence.
- **Record material use where it affects reproducibility.** If someone repeating your work needs to
  know a tool was used to derive something, say so in the project record, along with what was
  checked.[^src-ai-playbook-accuracy] Spell-checking a paragraph is not material. Generating the
  transformation logic behind a published figure is.

::: {.callout-note title="Where the detailed AI guidance lives" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
Detailed guidance on building and assuring AI systems is in the AI estate that
[the standards landscape](r8-the-standards-landscape.qmd) points at. What this
page answers is the narrower question: what changes about **your** accountability when you use a
tool to help you work. Nothing does.
:::
